name: North Sikkim
tagline: Yak country, high lakes and Lepcha valleys
meta_description: Plan North Sikkim honestly: Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen, Gurudongmar and Dzongu, permits via registered operators, altitude safety and real 2026 prices.
summary: North Sikkim is the Mangan district above Gangtok: Lachung and Yumthang to the east, Lachen and Gurudongmar Lake (≈ 5,430 m) to the north, and the Lepcha reserve of Dzongu by the Teesta. Every trip needs a permit through a registered operator, and roads close often, so check current status before you travel.
intro: North Sikkim is the biggest and emptiest district of the state. Since 2021 it has been called Mangan district, after its small headquarters town on the Teesta. The 2011 census counted about 43,700 people in an area larger than the other districts, so most of what you see is forest, river gorge, moraine and snow. The road climbs from about 1,000 m at Mangan to 5,430 m at Gurudongmar Lake in a single day's drive, which is the first thing every traveller here needs to understand.

There are two valleys that most people come for. The Lachung valley runs east to Yumthang, the rhododendron meadows of the Shingba sanctuary and, on a good day, Zero Point at Yume Samdong. The Lachen valley runs north past Thangu to Gurudongmar Lake, close to the Tibetan plateau. Both villages are run by their own traditional councils, the Dzumsa, and both live on tourism, apples, potatoes, yak and sheep.

Lower down, the Teesta cuts through Lepcha country. Dzongu, across the river from Mangan, is a reserve where only Lepchas may own land. You need a separate permit and you stay in family homestays, not hotels. On the highway from Gangtok you also pass Kabi Lungchok, where Lepcha and Bhutia leaders swore blood brotherhood, and Phodong, one of the six main monasteries of Sikkim.

We will be straight with you about access. The October 2023 glacial lake outburst flood destroyed the Teesta-III dam at Chungthang and long stretches of road. Lachen stayed shut to tourists for most of the next three years, and landslides in 2024, 2025 and 2026 closed Lachung and Lachen again for months at a time. Plans here must be flexible, and every booking should come with a fallback. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: The night South Lhonak broke
paras: South Lhonak is a glacial lake at about 5,200 m in the far north-west of the district. In 1977 satellite images showed it at about 17 hectares. As the Lhonak glacier retreated, it grew, and by 28 September 2023 it covered about 167 hectares. Scientists had listed it among the most dangerous lakes in the Sikkim Himalaya, and in 2018 pipes carried up by yak were installed to start draining it. An early warning system was still being planned when the rains came.

In the first days of October 2023 Sikkim received several times its normal rainfall. On the night of 4 October the lake burst its moraine wall. A warning reached the Teesta-III dam at Chungthang around midnight, and the operators tried to open the gates, but the flood arrived first. The 1,200 MW dam was destroyed in minutes. Downstream the Teesta rose by 15 to 20 feet, through Dikchu, Singtam, Rangpo and into West Bengal and Bangladesh.

More than 90 people were confirmed dead within two weeks, among them Indian Army soldiers, and fifteen bridges were lost. For North Sikkim the flood rewrote the map: Chungthang was badly damaged, the road to Lachen was cut, and Lachen did not reopen to tourists until March 2026, after the new Taram Chu bridge was built. That is why we ask you to treat every North Sikkim plan as provisional.
story.source: Wikipedia, '2023 Sikkim flash floods' and 'South Lhonak Lake'; EastMojo reporting on the Lachen reopening, March 2026

did_you_know: Gurudongmar Lake sits at 5,430 m according to the Government of Sikkim, which makes it one of the highest lakes in the world that tourists can drive to.
The Teesta is born up here: Tso Lhamo lake, about 5 km from Gurudongmar, is counted as its source, and the river joins its Lachen and Lachung arms at Chungthang.
The botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker walked up the Lachen valley in May 1849 and later went into the Lachung valley, collecting rhododendron seed that ended up in English gardens.
Lachen and Lachung govern themselves through the Dzumsa, a village council headed by an elected Pipon, which the Sikkim government formally recognised in 2001.
Dzongu was declared a reserve for the Lepcha people by a royal proclamation of the Chogyal in 1956, and outsiders still need a special permit to enter.

highlights.title: Yumthang in rhododendron season
highlights.text: From late April into May the Shingba Rhododendron Sanctuary around Yumthang (3,564 m) flowers in reds, pinks, whites and yellows. Go early in the morning from Lachung, 24 km away, before cloud fills the valley, and add Zero Point if your permit and the road allow it.

highlights.title: Gurudongmar at dawn
highlights.text: The drive from Lachen starts at about 4 am and climbs past Thangu to a lake at 5,430 m, sacred to Buddhists and linked by legend to Guru Padmasambhava. Twenty to thirty minutes at the shore is enough; the altitude is the real story of the day.

highlights.title: A Lepcha homestay in Dzongu
highlights.text: Across the Teesta from Mangan, Dzongu is a Lepcha reserve of cardamom groves, rice terraces and hot springs. You sleep in family homes, eat what the farm grows and walk to villages with a local guide. It needs its own permit.

highlights.title: Lachung and its Dzumsa
highlights.text: Lachung is a village of wooden houses, apple trees and prayer flags at about 2,700 m, run by its own council of elders and an elected Pipon. Walk up to the 1880 Lachung Monastery and ask your host how the Dzumsa works.

highlights.title: Snow without an expedition
highlights.text: From December to March, snow usually lies around Lachung and on the road to Yumthang. For many families from the plains this is the easiest place in India to touch deep snow, but expect closures after fresh falls.

highlights.title: The highway's history stops
highlights.text: Between Gangtok and Mangan stop at Kabi Lungchok, where the Lepcha-Bhutia blood brotherhood was sworn, at Phodong Monastery and at the Seven Sisters Waterfall. Each is a short halt that turns a long transfer day into a story.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), both in Siliguri, and go up to Gangtok: about 115 km, 4–5 h by shared jeep or reserved car. North Sikkim trips start from Gangtok. Tourists cannot self-drive or take shared jeeps beyond the permit checkposts; you travel in a registered local vehicle with a local driver, booked through a registered operator who also files your permit. Gangtok to Lachung is about 120–125 km and Gangtok to Lachen about 129 km, each 6–7 h on a good day. Mangan, Kabi, Phodong and Singhik need no Protected Area Permit for Indians and can be reached by shared jeep from Gangtok. Under the September 2026 order, vehicles must cross the Toong checkpost by 4 pm in both directions. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian citizens need a Protected Area Permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen, Thangu and Gurudongmar. It is applied for only through a registered Sikkim tour operator, with ID and photos, usually a few days in advance, and same-day permits are not issued. Foreign nationals need a Restricted Area Permit through an approved operator, travel in groups of two or more, and are not allowed to Gurudongmar Lake; they can usually go as far as Thangu. Dzongu needs its own permit for every non-Lepcha visitor, usually arranged by your homestay. Rules change often; check current status before you travel.

budget.summary: The cheapest honest way to see North Sikkim is a shared group package from Gangtok: a seat in a Bolero or Xylo, a basic hotel, all meals and the permit in one price. Private cars cost three to four times as much per person unless you fill them. Travel in shoulder weeks such as early March, late May or November, sleep in Lachung or Lachen family hotels, and skip extras like Zero Point unless the day is clear.
tips: Book a group package for the Lachen–Lachung loop and a private car only for the Gangtok sightseeing days.
Rent snow boots and padded jackets in Lachung for ₹150–300 an item instead of buying gear you will wear twice.
Pay for Zero Point on the morning itself, once your driver confirms the road is open and the sky is clear.
Carry cash from Gangtok or Mangan, because ATMs further north are few and often out of service.
Avoid Indian school holidays in late May and Puja week in October, when hotel rates in Lachung jump.

months.weather: Lachung −8 to 5 °C, dry, snow on the ground
months.summary: January is deep winter. Lachung usually has snow, and the road to Yumthang is open on most days only as far as the snow allows. Lachen and Gurudongmar are often blocked after snowfall, and the lake is frozen solid. Days are clear and cold; nights in unheated rooms drop well below zero. It is a good month for a snow trip to Lachung if you accept that a fresh fall can close the road for a day or two.
months.tip: Pick a hotel with heated mattresses or electric blankets and confirm it in writing.
months.price_note: Outside New Year week, rates are low and group packages run with fewer seats filled.

months.summary: February is still snow season, with the heaviest falls often late in the month. Losar, the Tibetan new year, falls in February or early March, and Lachung and Lachen households celebrate it at home and in the gompas. Roads above Lachung and to Gurudongmar can be shut for days. Pack for −10 °C at dawn and keep a buffer day in Gangtok in case the permit office halts trips after snow.
months.tip: Ask your operator to watch the weather forecast and move the North Sikkim days rather than cancel.
months.price_note: Rates stay low, except around Losar when some family hotels close for the holiday.

months.weather: Lachung −2 to 11 °C, clearing, snow on high ground
months.summary: March is a turning month. Snow still lies at Yumthang and Zero Point, but the lower valleys warm up and the first rhododendrons open at lower altitudes by the end of the month. Lachen reopened to tourists in March 2026 after the Taram Chu bridge was built, so this is also when the northern road is first tested each year. Clear mornings make it good for mountain views from Singhik.
months.tip: If you want both snow and some flowers, aim for the last ten days of March.
months.price_note: Shoulder-season prices hold until Holi week, when Bengal and Delhi families arrive.

months.weather: Lachung 2 to 15 °C, mostly clear mornings, afternoon cloud
months.summary: April is one of the two best months. The Shingba sanctuary begins to flower from late April, snow remains on the peaks around Yumthang, and Gurudongmar is usually reachable though still largely frozen. Afternoons cloud over and can bring hail, so start sightseeing early. Dzongu is green and warm, with orchids in the forest. Book Lachung hotels ahead for the last week of April.
months.tip: Leave Lachung for Yumthang by 6 am; flowers photograph best before the cloud.
months.price_note: Rates rise in the second half of the month as the flower season starts.

months.weather: Lachung 6 to 18 °C, clear mornings, pre-monsoon showers
months.summary: May is peak rhododendron month at Yumthang and the busiest month of the year. Gurudongmar starts to thaw at the edges by the end of the month. Pre-monsoon storms can bring landslides from mid-May, as they did in 2025, so keep a buffer day. Saga Dawa, the month of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death, often begins in late May and is marked in the gompas.
months.tip: Book early and avoid the Indian summer school holidays if you can.
months.price_note: The most expensive month; hotels in Lachung often sell out and group seats fill a week ahead.

months.summary: June is when the monsoon arrives and North Sikkim becomes risky. In June 2025 landslides cut roads to Lachen, Lachung and Chungthang, stranding more than 1,600 tourists, and an army camp at Chaten was hit. Permits are often suspended through the monsoon. If a trip is allowed, the valleys are green and full of primulas, but we do not sell North Sikkim tours in June and July.
months.tip: If you are in Sikkim now, stay on the Gangtok side and visit Phodong and Kabi instead.
months.price_note: Rates fall, but cancellation risk is high; take only refundable bookings.

months.summary: July is the heart of the monsoon, with daily rain, leeches in the lower forests and frequent slides on the North Sikkim Highway. Tourist permits for Lachung and Lachen are often suspended for weeks. The Teesta runs high and brown. Botanists and serious walkers sometimes come for the alpine flowers around Thangu, but it is not a month for a family holiday or a first visit.
months.tip: Treat any North Sikkim plan this month as unconfirmed until the morning you leave Gangtok.
months.price_note: Lowest rates of the year, with many Lachung hotels closed or running on skeleton staff.

months.weather: Lachung 10 to 18 °C, rain, breaks in the cloud
months.summary: August is still monsoon. On 8 August Sikkim keeps a state holiday for Tendong Lho Rumfaat, the Lepcha prayer to Mount Tendong, and Dzongu villages mark it with prayers and gatherings. Roads remain unreliable. In 2026 the Lachen road was only restored at the end of August after months of closure. Come only if you are flexible and stay low.
months.tip: If you go to Dzongu now, ask your homestay about the road to Sanklang before you set off.
months.price_note: Very quiet; homestays welcome guests but road risk is the hidden cost.

months.weather: Lachung 7 to 16 °C, rain easing late in the month
months.summary: September is the reopening month. In 2025 permits for Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point resumed on 8 September, and in 2026 permits for Lachen resumed around 10–11 September. Rain usually eases in the second half, and the alpine meadows around Yumthang and Thangu are at their greenest. Expect checkpost time limits and repair works on the road.
months.tip: Book the North Sikkim part for the last ten days of September, not the first.
months.price_note: Hotels discount to restart the season, and group departures are easy to join.

months.summary: October is the clearest month of the year and the start of the main season. Mountain views are sharpest, Gurudongmar is open and not yet frozen, and the maples and larches above Lachung begin to turn colour. Durga Puja and Diwali bring heavy demand from Kolkata and the rest of India, so book early. Nights fall to near zero in Lachung and well below at Thangu.
months.tip: If you can, travel the week after Puja rather than during it.
months.price_note: Puja week is the second peak after May; other weeks are moderately priced.

months.summary: November brings cold, dry, clear weather and thin crowds. Autumn colour lingers around Lachung, and Gurudongmar starts to freeze from the edges; the lake is usually frozen over by late in the month. Early snow can fall on the passes. It is our favourite month for budget travellers who want clear skies without the Puja crowd, provided they pack properly for the cold.
months.tip: Pack thermals, a down jacket, gloves and a woollen cap; nights at Lachen dip below zero.
months.price_note: Rates ease after Diwali and group departures still run daily from Gangtok.

months.summary: December usually brings the first proper snow to Lachung. Zero Point is often closed from mid-December. Phodong Monastery holds its masked chaam dances on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth Tibetan month, usually in December, just before Losoong, the Sikkimese harvest new year. Christmas and New Year week is busy and expensive; the first half of the month is quiet.
months.tip: Fix your Phodong visit to the chaam dates once the Tibetan calendar for the year is published.
months.price_note: Cheap until about 20 December, then New Year rates kick in.

faqs.q: Is North Sikkim open for tourists now
faqs.a: As of early October 2026, yes, with conditions. Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point reopened in September 2025, and permits for Lachen and Gurudongmar resumed around 10–11 September 2026 after the road near Taram Chu was repaired. Vehicles must cross the Toong checkpost by 4 pm in both directions. Landslides can close any of these at short notice, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Lachung and Lachen without a tour operator
faqs.a: No. Tourist permits for Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen and Gurudongmar are issued only through registered Sikkim tour operators, and you must travel in a registered local vehicle with a local driver. You cannot self-drive or ride shared jeeps past the checkposts. You can still keep costs low by joining a shared group package from Gangtok, which includes the permit, vehicle seat, hotel and meals.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for North Sikkim
faqs.a: Two nights is the minimum for both valleys: one night in Lachen for Gurudongmar and one in Lachung for Yumthang. One night in Lachung alone works for Yumthang only. Add at least one night in Gangtok before and after, because the drives are 6–7 hours and landslides can delay you. With young children or older parents, we suggest Lachung only, or two nights in Lachen before going higher.

faqs.q: Is Gurudongmar Lake safe for children and seniors
faqs.a: It is the highest point of most Sikkim trips at 5,430 m, so it needs care. Children under five should not go, and anyone with heart or lung conditions, high blood pressure or a recent illness should consult a doctor first. Everyone else should sleep a night in Lachen, drink water, avoid alcohol, move slowly and stay only 20–30 minutes at the lake. Turn back if anyone feels unwell.

faqs.q: How much does a North Sikkim trip cost from Gangtok
faqs.a: In 2026 a shared group package for Lachen and Lachung, two nights and three days with all meals, costs roughly ₹6,000–9,000 per person. A one-night Lachung group trip is about ₹3,500–5,500. A private car for the two-night loop costs about ₹16,000–22,000, plus hotels. Zero Point is extra, about ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle. These are indicative; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit North Sikkim
faqs.a: April–May for rhododendrons and lingering snow, and October–November for clear views and dry weather. December to March is for snow lovers who accept closures, especially on the Lachen side. June to August is monsoon, when landslides close roads and permits are often suspended. September is a reopening month; plan for its last ten days rather than the first.

Yes, with a Restricted Area Permit applied through an approved Sikkim operator, travelling in a group of at least two. Foreign nationals can usually visit Lachung and Yumthang and go up the Lachen valley as far as Thangu, but they are not permitted at Gurudongmar Lake. Zero Point rules for foreigners have varied. Dzongu needs a separate permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What did the 2023 flood change in North Sikkim
faqs.a: The South Lhonak glacial lake outburst of 4 October 2023 destroyed the Teesta-III dam at Chungthang, washed away bridges and long stretches of road, and cut off Lachen for most of three years. Lachung reopened earlier but was closed again by landslides in 2024 and 2025. Today roads are narrower, some bridges are single-lane, and checkpost time limits apply.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Mangan, Phodong and Kabi
faqs.a: Indian citizens do not need a Protected Area Permit for Kabi Lungchok, Phodong, Mangan or Singhik, which lie on the open stretch of the North Sikkim Highway. You can reach them by shared jeep from Gangtok. Dzongu, across the Teesta from Mangan, needs its own entry permit, and everything beyond the Toong checkpost needs the North Sikkim permit through an operator.
